review_text: We used the agency, Patagonia Experience, for this climb up the Villarica volcano. They provided a high level of technical equipment from the obvious essentials, such as ice axe and crampons, to the not so obvious add ons, including boots, rucksack, sunglasses, and inner and outer gloves. We were fitted for these the previous day so that when we arrived for our climb we were ready to go. Our group of six punters and two mountaineers (Joaquim and Pepo) were aged from twenty to sixty-one. All of the punters claimed to have a certain level of fitness although none had any specific mountaineering experience. All of our group opted to take the chair up to the first level which saved about forty minutes of uphill walking on volcanic scree, and cost 9000 Chilean Peso per person. This took us to the snow level, where the guides fitted the crampons onto everyone's feet. We then walked slowly, step by step, taking regular breaks for refreshment (which we kept in our rucksacks) up the volcano. Toilet stops for men were, as usual, not an issue. Ladies had to squat over a snow hole, beautifully dug to the correct size and shape by the guide, who had presumably sized us up in advance! The steady climb becomes more challenging about forty minutes from the top, when the slopes get steeper and the snow, deeper. At this point one of our party needed to rest more often, so our guide, Pepo, stayed with her while the rest of us carried on. Needless to say, on arriving at the top, the view and the euphoria of achieving your goal contribute to that 'top of the world' feeling. Lack of oxygen and the smell of volcanic fumes may also have been a contributing factor! After thirty minutes of taking the usual photos (ice axes in the air and jumping wearing crampons!) we began our trek down, firstly walking in deep snow. We then stopped to remove our crampons and take a 'nappy' and soft 'plastic tray' from our Mary Poppins style ruck sacks. The rest of our descent used these to slide through the snow and ice until we reached the volcanic scree level. Although this was not as physically tiring, it was hard work and careering down a slope with just an ice axe for a break is not everyone's idea of fun! The day finished back at Patagonia Experience with beer and biscuits. Our guides were superb. Joaquim and Pepo adopted just the right combination of skill, knowledge, tuition and encouragement. We had confidence in them. Joaquim told us afterwards that all he needs to get people to the top is a good level of fitness and determination. I would highly recommend Patagonia Experince and this activity - it was hard but an experience that I will never forget.

review_text: We've been living in Chile for five years and have been on many tours in various valleys. Typically the tours are quite reasonably priced as they attract people who later buy the wine and stay for lunch. Although the area where the tour takes place is very scenic (looking over the valley) and the building is beautiful, the tour itself was very basic, group was very large, tasting mediocre (Equilibrio, which costs 16.000 per person), etc. Normally tastings tempt you with at least one high end wine that makes you want to buy a few bottles before leaving (as often you can't get some of the bottles anywhere else), but this was not the case. We didn't buy one bottle as nothing was that interesting or original in the tasting. In summary, the tasting was very disappointing and VERY expensive overall. Would recommend going to the restaurant and skipping the tasting all together.

review_text: A lot of tour companies arrange excursion to the La Sebastiana combining with vina del Mars wine tour outside of Santiago. Since we are not too crazy about wine tasting, we traveled there utilizing public transit.We took the Metro to U de Santiago Station which is on #1 subway line catching a bus to Valparasio. Pullman ( Nicer and only few dollars more expensive)or Tur-bus go there. They have a separate line for Valaparasio which is shorter, so make sure you are lining up for that. Also, get the seats on the left side it is more scenic. From the bus station you can take a long walk to La Sebastiana but we took a taxi there (about$5) We enjoy touring the poet's house very much even though we do not know the poet and his poems at all before. The English audioguide is very well organized, informative and allow us to tour around at our own pace. The house is unique and the whimsical collections are very interesting. The hilly town of Valparasio is worth wondering around too. After visiting La Sebatiana, we have a nice walk around town and enjoying the outdoor murals and view. Also, we have our best meal for this Chile and Argentina trip at Cafe Turri .We were so glad that we went on our own!

review_text: A friend recommended Erasmo (aka “The Reserve of Caliboro”) and we learned more about it from MOVI the newly established organization of small wine producers in Chile (more info below). It made for a pleasant and very memorable afternoon, and we are very glad that we visited! This historic bodega (winery) and its diverse varietal organic vineyards are a bit off the beaten track, (about 3 hours South of Santiago and then 45 minutes to the West of Ruta 5 Sur), but the drive is easy and quite beautiful. It's also a convenient stop on a trip to or from the South of Chile. Erasmo's website has a map and turn by turn instructions which you'll want to print and take with you (click the button to view it in English). The property which has 230 hectares (568 acres) is the nucleus of one of the original great fundos of Chile which was over 54,000 acres! We especially liked seeing the enormous centerpiece vine of their grape arbor with its massive trunk that dates back 150 years to the time when the bodega was originally constructed. The property is now owned by Italian Count Francesco Marone Cinzano who splits his time between Chile and Tuscany where he is also a noted producer of the Col d'Orcia wines. Hopefully, we can someday visit this beautiful place in our travels as well. Because of its distance from Santiago, Erasmo receives relatively few visitors so the tours aren't as polished as say Concha y Toro, but unlike the large highly commercialized bodegas they're happy tailor your tour to whatever interests you the most. It helps to have a bit of Spanish if you want to understand the finer points, but you'll be well received no matter what language you speak. What Erasmo might lack in polish is more than compensated by its authenticity. The 150 acres of certified organically grown grapes are still hand picked and made into wines in small or even micro lots to bring out the highest potential of each. The unique soils of the property, coupled with organic dry cultivation results in rich full bodied wines which we think show exceptional character. We'd suggest making contact by telephone (in Spanish) or by email (English, Spanish or Italian) to tell them that you're coming. (We've found that generally our hosts at hotels or B&B's have been quite happy to make the arrangements for us by telephone.) It is possible to have lunch at the bodega if you wish. If you're lucky, you may even get to meet and dine with the Count as we did. We found him to be well informed on a wide variety of subjects and we had a very enjoyable conversation (in English!) that ranged through the history of the property, the cultivation of the vineyards, styles of wine and current events. Lunch was prepared mostly with ingredients grown on the property. It was very good - oso bucco, favas, fresh baked bread, a nice dessert with fresh strawberries and of course 4 different Erasmo wines; their signature Barrel Selection, unique (and delicious) Barbera Garnacha, a really good 2003 Cabernet Sauvignon from their wine library and an excellent Late Harvest Torontel for dessert. Spectacular! Finally, Erasmo is a founding member of MOVI. For those like us who may just be learning about the wines of Chile. We want to say that we are very much impressed with this budding new Chilean organization of small (and very small) producers of fine wines. Their mission is to showcase the truly exceptional quality of wines that Chile can produce and their website has links to all of their members. This resource has yielded to us discoveries of some great wines we might never have known about otherwise. Now, back to the wine touring.....

review_text: Wonderful day with a fun group of tourists from around the world and the ever delightful Helen our Tour Guide and Jimmy the fearless driver. They picked up from the hotel and started through the rush-hour traffic of Santiago. This gave Helen a lot of time to give us History and insight into the City of 7 million people. On rest stop then up to 8500 feet in less then an hour from Santiago. What an incredible landscape from the reservoir that supplies water to this dessert region of Chile. As the Andes rise another 4000 ft off in the distance. The bird life around the reservoir is unique, the landscape is giant and more similar to the surface of the moon versus the Rockies. Dust clouds kicked up just as we finished lunch. brushing the slopes of fine pebbles. The Empanada's at the end were a nice touch. Helen was very informative and a lot of fun as she set up lunch ad kept our wine glasses full. This was a highlight for my wife and I. You need 500 pesos to use the Banos at the last rest stop!!! review_text: A sobering but fascinating account of human rights abuses and violations during the infamous Pinochet regime. The museum is housed on three floors of a large modern building. Non-Spanish speakers can obtain an audio guide in English. It recounts the awful stories of the thousands of Chileans who were killed or who 'disappeared' during this dreadful, repressive period. Some of the tour is incredibly moving -- notably a huge three-storey wall covered by photos of the victims. It was dismaying to read about the relaxed, amiable attitude towards Pinochet by the British government at the time. We visited it on the first full day of our stay, and at the end of our holiday we felt it had explained and illuminated so much of Chilean life and politics in the present day.

review_text: After having read various comments we decided to go to Viu Manent as we only planned to visit a single winery. It's about a 2:30 hour drive from Santiago through the famous Ruta del Vino. We drove with a rented car and were glad to have a GPS on board as the road wine is not the easiest to find one out of the highway 5. Upon our arrival we were greeted by a friendly staff that took our reservation for the next tour and let us go around the winery to have a look. As we had time ahead of us we also visited the Colchagua Museum which is a very interesting place to visit with many exhibits from all over Chili tracing the country's history. Back to Viu Manent the entry ticket was 14000 pesos (about 22€) a fair price including a full tour with horse and carriage, visit of the winery and wine tasting from 4 different blends of red ( Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and 2 Merlots) and a fresh rosé. Cabernet Sauvignon was by far our preferred one and we could buy a pair at a very fair price. Our group was just the two of us (!) and our guide Juan-Miguel gave us a wonderful tour in English. We ended our tour by a late lunch at the restaurant who offers an excellent menu at reasonable prices, excellent service, great views of the vines and more wine tasting by the glass. A great and memorable experience to recommend to wine lovers and worth every penny of it!

review_text: It was the most magical experience of my life. Jorge, who has an excellent command of English, first gave us a brief background about astronomy: telling us about the history of the heliocentric model, as well as explaining to us about the numerous telescopes he had with him for us to try. Seeing the star-filled sky, both with the naked eye and using the telescopes, was unbelievably amazing. The skies were cloudless, and the stars filled the skies. Jorge, with his vast knowledge of astronomy, explained to us the positions of the planets and many of the stars and constellations. This made the stargazing extra enjoyable, as we were quickly able to identify objects such as Mars, Venus, the Orion belt, etc. To top it all off, his wife kindly made for us hot drinks (coffee, tea, hot chocolate, etc) and snacks (nachos, sandwiches, brownies, etc) and provided us with heaters and blankets to make us feel comfortable. All in all, a life changing experience which was so enjoyable!

review_text: This is not your average hiking park. First the drive to it is over gravel roads and although the park is close to Valdivia will take an hour plus to arrive as you have to go quite slowly. Park entrance fees are 3,000 pesos per person. Once you arrive the park doesn't have traditional hiking trails. You drive from trail to trail, stopping and parking and then hiking very short 20 min loops. Then you're off to do the next loop or just to stop for a picture spot. At the end of the drive/hike loop you finally get to a traditional hiking trail which is about an hour and a half return. Very easy climb (not much in the way of altitude gain from where you park). Filled with kids. The views at the top are beautiful and worth the trip but if you're seeking a 4-5 hour hike in solitude this isn't the place for you.

review_text: The termas have about ten different pools of natural hot water, some of them with a little fall, which acts as hydro massage, it's really great. The entrance fee for foreigners is 15000 pesos. The regular bus tours usually combine this with the geyser del tatio or something else and large group of people will come for a short period of time. Best thing to do is to get your own car to get there and spend some time, people will come and go and you will get the pool for yourself again. Note that it can be tricky to spot the entrance if you don't know it but you should see the parking with cars parked from the road. Locals tend to use the first two pools (top ones), so these get very crowded, the further you go, the less people there are. When you have had enough, there's an area with table and chairs where you can have a picnic.

review_text: We used Turistik for 3 days in Santiago, 2 for hop-on hop-off transportation, and one day trip to Valparaíso and Vina del Mar. Santiago traffic works against the best intentions of the hop-on bus, which is actually informative and as efficient as possible. But the traffic kills it. Our hotel was near stop1 Parque Arauco, so it made sense to use it to get to the historic district (stops 5-9 of 13). If I was staying closer to the historic district I would not advise the hop-on experience, except it made for an easy and smooth entrance to San Cristobel via gondola and funicular. But the day trip to Valparaíso and Vina del Mar was superb. Andrea was a great guide and the trip was informative, well paced, and unhurried. Nice lunch in Vina del Mar along with a tour of the downtown and a walk along the beach. In Valparaíso, a downhill walk through a funky neighborhood and lots of information about a neat city. Time from Santiago 9 hours (9 am to 6 pm) on a Saturday, without Santiago traffic. Good value as a way to see outside Santiago, Casablanca wine area, and coast. We appreciate your comment dear traveler, it is very important for us to know about your experience.

review_text: Santiago's metro system is easy to use, safe and clean. The system is quite extensive and it's a great way to travel around. Instead of buying single trip tickets, it's a good idea to purchase a smart card (called a "Bip!" card, after the noise it makes at the entry gates to the platforms). A Bip! card can also be used on the city's buses. The first section of the Santiago subway was built by a French company and the rolling stock runs on rubber tyres, similar to the system in Montreal and Paris. Many of the stations have very nice artistic interiors and the whole system is a great credit to the city of Santiago. Highly recommended transport option.

The off-bike activities were also wonderful because we got to see Fitz Roy, the Perito Moreno Glacier, and the Torres del Paine. Daniel and Felipe were not only true professionals in guiding us through Patagonia, but also terrific fellow riders to have on the tour as well. Whether it was chatting amongst us during pit stops in between long stretches of tarmac, or patiently shepherding us through difficult off-road sections, Daniel and Felipe enabled our group to ride safely and most importantly, to have fun. I will forever remember and cherish the memories created during this tour.

review_text: Our original plan was to visit the Laguna Cejar, having some fun in the water after the previous long lasting excursions. But Laguna Cejar was closed because of arsen concentration! Ok we decided to enter: it is a nice place with a total of 8 small pools in a real nice landscaping. The temperature of the water depends on its detailed location/level in that valley; the temperatures ranging between 28 down in the valley and 36C° up in the valley. The upper pools were completely reserved for the tour groups. Very relaxing, but even the prices are so high, in some periods the pozos were fully occupied and overcrowded. I do not understand why in those cases the access is not limited/ restricted, because there is not much you can do else here - business as usual. review_text: First of all, the W trek was amazing and I would highly recommend you do it. I would not recommend booking through Howlanders though. We received our packing list which did not include crampons and so left ours back in the UK. Howlanders then emailed to say we would need them but after we had already left for our trip. We asked if there were any we could borrow (given the cost of the tour, it seemed quite a small ask), but were informed we had to rent them. We therefore had to spend an additional $100 renting these in Puerto Natales only to find when we got to Torres del Paine, we didn't need them! Bad communication and bad information from Howlanders! Also you can easily book this trip yourself without going through a tour company and save yourself lots of money. My recommendation for East to West walk below: - Day 1 - Get an early bus to the central refugio and hike up to mirador del Torres that day. Stay at central refugio. - Day 2 - Walk from central refugio to refugio Frances, stay in refugio Frances - Day 3 - Walk up French Valley to view point, and then hike back down to Paine Grande refugio - Day 4 - Hike to Glacier Grey and back and get boat from Paine Grande that evening Doing this will also save you one night's accommodation in the national park vs the Howlanders tour which is very expensive. review_text: Chillán's modernist cathedral from around 1950 is a masterpiece by a visionary architect. Its round shapes and soft colors are manna for the soul - in fact, the church's 10 arches are an imitation of 10 fingers about to intertwine in prayer. Brilliant. The interior decoration is sparse, tasteful, and deeply surprising. Normally, in the Catholic tradition, Jesus is portrayed as a defeated, deeply suffering, and heavily bleeding figure. In this church, we get an alternative image of God's son - as a strong and cheerful young man who has surplus for those around him. He is the Savior, who handles matters for all in need. Beautifully thought out. Of the many hundreds of churches I have seen in many countries around the world, this is the most beautiful and inspiring. A huge detour worth it, if you are in this area (Chillán city, on the other hand, is a very unexciting place to stay).

review_text: Overall this trip was a great experience and we are glad we did it. The white flats are just stunning and our driver Vladi went above and beyond to make sure we got some super cool pictures. He was a great driver and we always felt super safe. The thermal baths on the first day were great (although if you know you get altitude sickness worth giving them a miss, I got really bad altitude sickness on the first day and I don't think going in the baths helped) The wildlife and landscapes we saw were amazing (wild flamingos were a highlight). Accomodation, the first night was pretty basic, but it was clean and had a warm shower. Second night was lovely. Food, we struggled slightly with some of the food. I think this is due to the remote area we were traveling in rather than the company used. The lunches the driver made us were quite good. The meals we got at the hotels were less good, we had chips both nights which were cold and super greasy. I actually missed the meal on the first night due to altitude sickness but the other veggies said the veggie option was some kind of potatoe cake with cold chips. The second night was fried aubergine, which again was so greasy I couldn't eat it. On the second morning we had one pre made pancake each for breakfast, suited me as felt fragile from altitude sickness, but my husband struggled. I wouldn't let it put you off going just pack plenty of snacks-especially for the evening meals. The one thing that really let this trip down for us (and the reason for the 3 stars) was the guide. We paid extra for an English speaking guide (as despite trying our best on Duolingo our Spanish is very limited).It became clear early on that Carla didn't know a lot about the area, and that perhaps this was her first time visiting. Therefore the information we got was very limited. Our driver seemed to have a lot of info to share, but as Carla's English was limited, she was unable to share a lot of this information with us. Totally get that we are in a Spanish speaking county and the responsibility to learn the language is on us, however after paying quite a bit more than the rest of the group so we could have an English guide, the lack of information we got was disappointing. There was another guide Omar who was traveling in tandem with us with another tour. He seemed a lot more knowledgeable and at some spots we were able to tag a long with his group which was great. Carla seemed lovely and was kind whilst I was sick, but we essentially didn't get the service we paid extra for which was such a shame.

review_text: I really enjoyed this. You meet at their office and take a short drive to the edge of San Pedro de Atacama, where you are met by someone who tells you about the stars. There is a very interesting 45 minute talk about the stars, which sticks strictly to the scientific side and then you get a chance to look at the stars through a telescope. They limit the group size to ten, and there are four telescopes. Two people were no-shows on our trip which was good for us. Each telescope is looking at something different and you take it in turns peering thorough each one. With such a small group everyone got a decent look. Our tour was in English, the man who told us about the stars was very interesting, extremely knowledgeable and willing to answer lots of questions. I can’t remember his name but he was tall and I think he had a Dutch accent. He was very good. Oh, and they dropped us back where we were staying. I really cannot think how the tour could have been better unless you personally hired an astronomer and had a telescope all to yourself. But I don’t think anyone, unless they already had a specialist interest, would need that. I really do recommend this tour. I have lived all my life in big European cities, I have never seen so many stars.

review_text: This museum has an excellent website with lots of good documents and photos - much in English so expectations were high. The top floor is an excellent summary of Mexico to Chile pre-columbian cultures - essentially by era and by culture with timelines and maps and great explanations - some in English. The scope of art media is textiles ( cotton, llama, feathers - woven, knit, embroidered, tie died etc), metal, wood, ceramics and stone. There is a section of just the 'masterpieces'. It is a balanced picture of all the cultures not weighted towards one region. Pieces are well selected and well displayed with photography allowed, except understandably, not for most of the textiles. The basement features the peoples of Chile including desert cultures subject to Incas in 1400s to a bit on Easter Island ("Rapa Nui"), but the primary focus on the Mapuche in Central and south Chile. Minor complaint is that the basement displays are not well lit, making viewing and reading difficult. Worth a 2.5 hour visit

review_text: From Puerto Montt/Varas, we took a bus to Cochamo and asked to be dropped at "La Junta". If you plan to camp, buy all the food you need in Puerto Montt/Varas because there is no food to buy in the valley!! From the road where the bus drops you, there is 6,5 km to Quila (the first camping and the beginning of the trek in the valley). You can either walk them, pay a lift or hitchhike if you're lucky as we were. We slept in Quila camping for 5000 pesos, there is no accommodation except a toilet. The next day we started the trek in the valley to la Junta 11 km, 2,5-3h. There it's also possible to camp. The place is wonderfull ! 10 min walk and a naked foot river crossing from there, there is the famous toboganes. It's beautiful, you can try to slide them. It's not so dangerous if you start from upper left (there's a rope to grab), but be prepared for freezing water haha!! We also climbed to the mirador cerro Arcoiris. It's a challenging climb with rope climbing at the end. Was funny but stay focused to not fall! View on top amazing!

I'd be willing to pay more to have a private experience.

review_text: This park is amazing. Getting here from Puerto Natales by car is a rough ride with lots of alternating sections of paved and unpaved rocky, bumpy roads...also, remember to bring your passport when you pay your entrance fee, especially if you want to return in the following 2 days with the same ticket. You must pay in CLP or dollars. They do not accept credit cards. I would plan to arrive very early or mid morni g to avoid the buses of tourists in line to pay their entrance fees. The ranger must stamp the ticket and you have to bring show your passport again. We enjoyed exploring the park by car because you could stop as frequently as you wanted for the never ending photo opportunities. All roads in the park were unpaved but not terribly bumpy. We especially enjoyed the waterfall hike at salto grande. We did several shorter hikes so we could experience more of the park in a single day. Had we used our entire day to hike to the Torres, you don't experience the amazing views until you reach the top. We heard from several people that the French side of the W was the best hike, but again a full day trek. Bring your own food and water because we did not see other options. Also, gas up car before you leave Puerto natales since we didn't passant gas stations. This park was well worth the effort to get here!

He gives you all sorts of history about Pucon, the volcano, and even ends the tour with recommendations/local advice for activities for the remainder of your stay as well as good restaurants and shopping. Javi went even above and beyond by taking those who were interested to lunch after to talk more about the town/life in general. We liked Javi so much that we went to see him play live music later in the evening and then enjoyed beers and pizza together after! Easily, 5 stars for this tour! Logistics: We met for the tour at 11am near the tourist info booth in the central park. Javi was there promptly at 11 and we were off on the tour shortly after.
